location.value: The Japanese islands plus colonies: Taiwan (from 1895), Karafuto (southern Sakhalin, from 1905), Korea (annexed 1910) and the South Seas Mandate. It occupied large parts of China and Southeast Asia in the 1930s–40s.

terrain.value: A mountainous island chain with limited farmland and few raw materials, a reason it sought resources overseas.
terrain.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

resources.value: Few domestic resources (some coal, silk). It depended on imported oil, iron and rubber, which drove expansion into Manchuria and Southeast Asia.
resources.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

disasters.value: The Great Kantō earthquake (1923) devastated Tokyo and Yokohama and was followed by a massacre of Korean residents. The US firebombing of cities and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1945).

population.value: 77.7 million (1920) and 105.2 million (1940) including colonies. The home islands had 56.0 and 73.1 million respectively (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Tokyo (capital from 1869) and Osaka grew into major industrial cities.
urbanisation.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

disease.value: Public health modernised. Wartime shortages caused hunger and disease by 1944–45.
disease.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

migration.value: Japanese settlers moved to Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria and the Americas. Many Koreans and Chinese were brought to Japan, often as forced labour during the war.
migration.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

economicBase.value: Rapid industrialisation from the Meiji era: textiles, then shipbuilding, steel and arms, led by large business groups (zaibatsu).
economicBase.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

tradeRoutes.value: Silk and textile exports, and imports of raw materials. Colonies and Manchuria were organised as an imperial economic bloc (the “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere”).
tradeRoutes.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

wealth.value: The first non-Western country to industrialise. No GDP figure is given in the sources checked.
wealth.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

moneyAndTax.value: The yen (from 1871), plus colonial Korean and Taiwanese yen. The Meiji land tax reform (1873) financed modernisation.

inequality.value: Zaibatsu owners and landlords prospered, while tenant farmers and workers were poor, which fuelled unrest in the 1920s–30s.
inequality.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy (1868–1889), then a semi-constitutional monarchy under the Meiji Constitution (1889). From 1940 to 1945 it was ruled by an ultranationalist authoritarian regime.

keyRulers.value: Emperors Meiji (1868–1912), Taishō (1912–1926) and Shōwa/Hirohito (1926–1989). Prime ministers Itō Hirobumi (first, 1885) and Tōjō Hideki (1941–44).

succession.value: Hereditary imperial line. Real power lay with oligarchs, cabinets and, increasingly, the military.
succession.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

institutions.value: The Charter Oath (1868), the Meiji Constitution (1889), the Imperial Diet (from 1890), universal conscription, and compulsory education.

stability.value: The Boshin War (1868–69), the Satsuma Rebellion (1877), the “Taishō Democracy” of the 1910s–20s, and political assassinations and military coup attempts in the 1930s (e.g. 1936).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between civilian politicians and the army and navy, and between army factions, which increasingly controlled policy in the 1930s.
eliteConflict.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

armyAndTech.value: A modern conscript army and navy built on Western models. Aircraft carriers and naval aviation by the 1930s–40s.
armyAndTech.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

majorWars.value: The First Sino-Japanese War (1894–95), the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05), the First World War, the Mukden Incident and occupation of Manchuria (1931), the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–45), and the Pacific War (attack on Pearl Harbor, 1941).

territoryChange.value: Area 1.98 million km² (1938), rising to about 7.4 million km² at its wartime peak (1942). All colonies and conquests were lost in 1945.

alliancesRivals.value: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902–23), then the Axis with Germany and Italy (the Tripartite Pact, 1940). Rivals: China, Russia/the USSR, and the US.

inventions.value: Rapid adoption of Western technology: railways, telegraph, shipbuilding and, later, advanced aircraft and warships.
inventions.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

scienceEducation.value: Compulsory primary education gave Japan high literacy. Imperial universities (Tokyo, 1877). Scientists such as Kitasato Shibasaburō.
scienceEducation.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

openness.value: Very open to Western learning in the Meiji era (the Iwakura Mission). It became nationalist and closed in the 1930s, with heavy censorship and propaganda.

religion.value: A secular state on paper, but State Shinto, centred on worship of the emperor, served as state ideology. Buddhism was also present.

languageWriting.value: Japanese, which was imposed in the colonies (e.g. Korean name-change and language policies).

artsArchitecture.value: Meiji Western-style architecture, and writers such as Natsume Sōseki and Akutagawa.
artsArchitecture.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

socialStructure.value: The old samurai class was abolished (1870s). Emperor, peerage, zaibatsu business elites, and farmers and workers. Colonial subjects were ranked below Japanese.
socialStructure.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

sharedIdentity.value: Emperor-centred nationalism (kokutai), promoted through schools and State Shinto. Motto from 1936: “Eight Crown Cords, One Roof”.

neighbours.value: Qing China and the Republic of China, Korea, Russia/the USSR, and European colonies in Southeast Asia.

ideasReligions.value: A model of non-Western modernisation that inspired Asian reformers. Pan-Asian ideas were also used to justify expansion.
ideasReligions.source: Gordon, A Modern History of Japan (3rd ed., 2014)

colonisation.value: A colonial power in Taiwan, Korea and Manchuria. Its wartime record includes atrocities such as the Nanjing Massacre (1937), forced labour, and the “comfort women” system of sexual slavery.

riseSignals.value: The Meiji Restoration (1868), rapid industrialisation, a strong state and military, and victories over China (1895) and Russia (1905).

peakPeriod.value: Its greatest extent in 1942 during the Pacific War.

declineSignals.value: Militarism and overextension in China, war with the US and Britain (from 1941), resource shortages, and defeats at Midway (1942) and after.

outcome.value: Defeat. Japan surrendered on 2 September 1945 after the atomic bombings and the Soviet declaration of war. Under Allied occupation, the 1947 Constitution replaced the empire with today’s Japan.

sources.value: Government records, censuses, and Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Allied archives. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (the infobox was read word for word). See also Gordon (2014).

overallCertainty.value: High for events. Wartime atrocity death tolls and the nature of the 1930s–40s regime are debated.
